executive_summary: EUR/SGD closed at 1.42738 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in Singapore dollars per euro, so a falling pair means a stronger Singapore dollar. It is 0.85% lower over one month, 3.47% over three months, 4.07% over six months and 5.36% over a year. That puts it at the 1st percentile of its 52-week closing range, only 7 pips above the 27 October closing low of 1.42666. The main story is one energy shock hitting the two economies in opposite ways. Dutch gas at EUR100/MWh is eating into a euro-area current account surplus that has already fallen to 1.5% of GDP, while an AI-driven export boom is widening Singapore's surplus, which is near 17% of GDP. On the fiscal side, France has a 10-year spread over Germany of about 155bp and a 2027 budget without a majority, while Singapore is AAA-rated and runs a surplus. Two differences from the single-currency views matter for this cross. Carry flips sign: the euro pays about 137.5bp a year against the US dollar, but it earns about 120bp over three-month SORA, so a short EUR/SGD position pays carry of about 14 pips a month. Dollar funding largely cancels: tighter dollar funding weighs on both currencies against the US dollar, so the drag mostly nets out here. The tactical stance is Bearish, conviction 2 (weighted score -0.215, overall confidence 54%). The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 3 (-0.315, confidence 56%), led by External Balance, Guidance and Fiscal. Spot already sits inside a four-touch support band at 1.41985-1.4333 and 256 pips below a falling 50-day average of 1.45293. Positioning is crowded on both legs: a 143,900-contract euro non-commercial short, and a Singapore dollar trade-weighted index (S$NEER) about 1.65% above the middle of its policy band. That makes a short squeeze in the first half of November the main risk. We would therefore sell rallies into 1.4330-1.4366, below the ten-touch 1.43658-1.45024 band that capped the mid-October rebound, rather than sell at spot. Targets are 1.4160 by 27 November and 1.4000 by 30 April 2027. Our reservation is about timing, not direction: selling at spot gives a reward-to-risk of only 0.68:1 against a 1.4415 stop.

market_context.valuation_assessment: The two valuation measures disagree, and neither points to a near-term reversal. On World Bank GDP-based PPP factors, fair value for EUR/SGD is about 1.1140, so the euro looks about 28% rich against the Singapore dollar; that gap mostly reflects Singapore's low measured price level relative to its income, has lasted for decades and is not a six-month target. BIS real effective exchange rates rank the Singapore dollar as the richer currency in real trade-weighted terms: SGD 115.04 in September 2026 (88th percentile since January 2024, second-highest in G10+SGD) against EUR 103.27 (67th percentile). So the cross is not cheap for a euro seller in real terms, and the Singapore dollar's rich valuation limits how far its advantage can be pushed. What spot at the 1st percentile prices is the euro's current energy and French-fiscal discount. It does not price further erosion of the euro-area current account towards 1.0% of GDP, or an ECB that delivers less than the curve expects. (The 52-week range is 1.42400-1.52175 intraday and 1.42666-1.51694 on closes; the range and percentile above are on closes, and spot is at the 3rd percentile intraday.)

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised carry is +120.3bp for a long EUR/SGD position: the ECB deposit rate of 2.50% minus three-month compounded SORA of 1.297% on 30 October. It is a gap between short rates, not a funding gap implied by quoted forwards; no EUR/SGD future is listed, and the two measures differ by the term premium and the cross-currency basis. A short EUR/SGD position pays it. The carry-to-vol ratio is not calculated because no exchange or free source quotes EUR/SGD implied volatility; as a realised-volatility substitute only, 120bp divided by 60-day realised volatility of 2.79% is about 0.43. Carry has not worked for the euro holder: over six months a long position earned about 60bp of carry against a 4.07% spot loss, and over a year about 120bp against a 5.36% loss. Singapore dollar holders are paid mainly through the rising S$NEER band rather than through interest; the band appreciates at about 1.25% a year, matching the carry, and the spot moves have been driven by the euro's energy and fiscal discounts on top of that. The forward points above are rate-gap-implied outrights (indicative only).

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On short rates the euro is ahead by about 120bp. The ECB deposit rate is 2.50% after the 29 October hold. Singapore has no policy rate, and three-month compounded SORA, the short rate its exchange-rate regime produces, was 1.297% on 30 October. On 30 October closes the 10-year gap is about 108bp: Bunds at 3.32% against Singapore government bonds at 2.24%. Neither central bank decides anything inside the four-week window. The ECB's next decision is 17 December, and no verified Singapore policy schedule is on file, although MAS's next statement is expected in late January. MAS left the slope, width and centre of the S$NEER band unchanged on 14 October, with the slope estimated at about 1.25% a year. That lifts the trade-weighted Singapore dollar at about the rate the carry pays a euro holder. So the two effects roughly cancel: the euro earns about 14 pips a month of carry, and the band's built-in appreciation of the Singapore dollar against its basket offsets it. With nothing able to reprice the gap before December, the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over the strategic horizon, only one scheduled decision can move the gap: the ECB's on 17 December, which comes with new staff projections. A 25bp hike to 2.75% would widen the euro's lead over SORA to about 145bp. But markets already price about 75bp of further ECB tightening, and our euro view thinks that is about 25bp too much, because the ECB's own projections show core HICP at 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028. On the Singapore side MAS does not set SORA. It follows US rates through the forward market, only partly: it rose from a 1.06% average in the second quarter to about 1.30% now. A Fed hike on 9 December would therefore narrow the euro's lead slightly. The band slope compounds to about 0.6% of Singapore dollar appreciation over six months, which offsets roughly the 0.6% of carry a euro holder earns. The two effects are about the same size, and net of what is priced the gap is unlikely to change much, so the factor stays Neutral. The mismatch between what each central bank is likely to deliver and what markets price is scored under Guidance & Credibility, so it is not counted twice.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth gap is wider here than on any other factor. Singapore's third-quarter GDP rose 5.4% y/y and 1.1% q/q, against 1.3% y/y and 0.4% q/q in the euro area, where France contracted 0.1%. Inflation runs the other way. Euro-area HICP was 3.8% in September, driven by energy at 18.9%, with core at 2.5%; MAS core inflation eased to 2.0%, inside MAS's 1.5-2.0% range. Singapore therefore has the strongest growth in G10+SGD with contained inflation. The euro area has an energy-driven overshoot that is eroding real incomes, with wages rising 2.5-2.8% against 3.8% inflation. Momentum also diverges: the euro-area flash composite PMI fell to 51.9 from 53.1, against 52.7 expected, while Singapore's non-oil domestic exports rose 68.4% y/y in September and its manufacturing PMI rose to 51.7. The pair is more sensitive to one side. The S$NEER band absorbs Singapore data surprises, so EUR/SGD reacts more to the 4 November euro-area HICP flash and the November PMIs than to Singapore's October export and inflation releases. The factor works through the stagflation discount on the euro, and the next four weeks of data are more likely to confirm that discount than reverse it, so it is Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months both economies slow, from very different starting points. MAS expects Singapore's positive output gap to narrow through 2027 and core inflation to ease noticeably from mid-2027. Export growth faces a high base as the AI-driven surge laps itself. That stops Singapore's data from driving the band, but its mix of growth and inflation stays the best in the set. The euro area faces the harder path. UBS expects HICP to peak at 4.1% in January 2027, growth in bank lending to firms slowed to 4.2% in September as credit standards tightened, and our euro view puts quarterly growth at only 0.1-0.2% in the fourth and first quarters. Euro-area growth data do not yet show a real-wage squeeze of about 1 percentage point, or the rise in energy costs since the ECB's September projections. The gap narrows from Singapore's side and worsens from the euro's, which nets to Bearish for EUR/SGD. Confidence is a touch lower than tactically because Singapore's slowdown narrows the advantage.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two currencies behave differently under stress. The euro is not a safe haven at present: risk aversion hurts it through higher energy prices and wider French spreads, and both were at work in October, when euro high-yield spreads widened to 3.48% from 2.94% a month earlier. The Singapore dollar is low-beta. In a global risk-off it weakens against the US dollar but outperforms high-beta and energy-exposed currencies as capital moves to a AAA-rated hub, and its band dampens the moves. The dated risk is the period after the 3 November US midterms, when the US has said strikes on Iran become possible. Brent was at US$117.64 on 30 October after two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz. An escalation hurts both oil importers, but the euro also takes the gas price and French spread effects, while Singapore offsets part of the hit through refining margins. A settlement would help the euro more. With the VIX at 17.2 at the 29 October close and 20.05 intraday on 30 October, risk appetite is wobbling rather than breaking. The near-term outcomes lean against the euro, so the factor is Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months a settlement is about as plausible as an escalation: talks resumed in Tehran on 26 October with regional mediators, and Qatari mediation is under way. The euro would gain strongly from a settlement because energy is the main reason it has underperformed, while the band would mute the Singapore dollar's response. An escalation that kept Hormuz disrupted would deepen the euro's energy discount and could bring safe-haven money into Singapore from the region. Credit spreads have room to widen and US equities are close to records, so a broad sell-off in risk assets would hurt the euro more than the Singapore dollar. A settlement, though, gives the euro the bigger upside. Using roughly the outcome weights in our euro view (energy-led risk-off 40%, muddle-through 35%, settlement 25%) and allowing for the larger euro gain in a settlement, the net is close to zero, so the factor is Neutral.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised by 0.03 on both horizons (tactical 0.06 to 0.09, strategic 0.16 to 0.19) because the two economies' external positions are moving in opposite directions under the same energy shock. The euro area's surplus is eroding under gas and oil import costs, while Singapore's is widening on electronics exports. That makes the gap more decisive for this cross than the default weight assumes.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The energy shock hits the two external balances in opposite ways. Dutch TTF gas traded at EUR100/MWh on 28 October for the first time since December 2022, with EU storage near 75%. The euro area ran a EUR16.1bn goods deficit in August, its largest since January 2023, as petroleum imports rose 20.7%, and its 12-month current account surplus has fallen to 1.5% of GDP (12 months to August, best available). Singapore's surplus is widening: the second-quarter current account was S$37.08bn against S$30.52bn a year earlier, the 2025 surplus was 16.7% of GDP, and September exports rose 68.4% on a 107.6% jump in electronics. Both economies import oil, but the euro area also carries the gas shock, while Singapore recovers part of its oil bill through refining and re-export margins. Direct trade between them is small next to either economy's total. IMF figures for 2024 give the euro area a $11.2bn goods surplus with Singapore (exports $29.0bn, imports $17.9bn), and Singapore's own records point the same way ($39.8bn of imports from the euro area, $29.4bn of exports). That bilateral flow slightly favours the euro, but it is dwarfed by the opposite direction of the two overall balances as winter gas demand begins, so the factor is Bearish for the pair.

A surplus near 17% of GDP means a steady net supply of foreign currency into Singapore, recycled through MAS reserves, GIC and Temasek and kept orderly by the rising band. Third-quarter exports accelerated from +46.1% in August to +68.4% in September, so the third-quarter surplus is likely to beat the second quarter's. The euro area's 12-month surplus has already fallen from EUR290bn to EUR250bn. With August's monthly figure at EUR9bn, the current pace points towards about 1.0% of GDP by early 2027, and analysts expect high gas prices for at least another year. Valuation is the caveat. GDP-based purchasing power parity makes the euro look expensive against the Singapore dollar, but that mostly reflects Singapore's low measured price level and is structural, not a target. In real effective terms the Singapore dollar is the richer of the two, at the 88th percentile against the euro's 67th. That limits how far Singapore's advantage can be pressed but does not reverse it. The factor is Bearish with the highest strategic confidence of the ten.

Singapore's gas exposure is priced off Asian LNG rather than TTF, so the Singapore dollar is not directly affected, and the result is negative for the pair. Step 3, Asian LNG up: Singapore dollar negative and euro mildly negative through the global gas link, so the net is muted. Step 4: in this conflict Brent and TTF have risen together, so the combined energy effect is negative for EUR/SGD, led by the gas channel.

tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Inflation & Growth (0.18) and Policy & Rates (0.24) are the heaviest factors. The first is Bearish and the second Neutral, so the -0.215 score comes from the growth-inflation gap plus a group of smaller euro-specific negatives. Singapore grew 5.4% y/y in the third quarter with core inflation at 2.0%. The euro area grew 1.3% with HICP at 3.8% and a composite PMI that fell to 51.9, and because the S$NEER band absorbs Singapore surprises, euro-area data move this cross more. Policy & Rates is Neutral because the euro's roughly 120bp lead over three-month SORA is matched by a band slope near 1.25% a year, and neither side has a decision before the ECB on 17 December. Our two standalone views reinforce each other: the euro ranks 10th of 11 and the Singapore dollar 6th, so the cross isolates the euro's energy and French discounts without the US dollar funding leg, which is why that factor's weight was cut. The two factors specific to this pair push the same way: the external balances diverge under the energy shock, and the fiscal gap is acute, between a French debt ratio of 119% with a budget lacking a majority and a AAA-rated surplus. The main offset is positioning. The euro's non-commercial net short of 143,900 contracts and a Singapore dollar about 1.65% above its band mid-point make short EUR/SGD a crowded trade on both legs, and a squeeze is the main tactical risk. Markets price a December ECB hike and an unchanged MAS band. They do not price a successful French censure, an S&P outlook cut or a post-midterm energy escalation, all of which would hurt the euro. The path of least resistance is lower but choppy. The dated catalysts are the 3 November midterms and French revenue vote, the 4 November HICP flash, the 17 November whole-budget vote, the 26 November ECB account, the 27 November S&P review, and Singapore's October export and inflation data in the second half of November (release dates not confirmed). Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the score rests on breadth, the crowded short could produce sharp rallies, and no scheduled policy decision falls inside the window to confirm or refute the view. It is not 1 because the energy, fiscal and growth channels are independent and all active at once.

Trade plan: sell into 1.4330-1.4366 (56-92 pips above spot), stop on a daily close above 1.4415, target 1.4160; breakdown alternative: sell a daily close below 1.4198, stop 1.4275 (about 1.2 ATR), target 1.4030, about 2.1:1; sizing at conviction 2 is half a standard risk unit (0.5% of capital at risk on the 65-pip stop gives notional of about 1.1 times capital).

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.315 is clearly Bearish. External Balance alone contributes -0.114, about 36% of the total. Guidance & Credibility (-0.066), Inflation & Growth (-0.054) and Fiscal (-0.052) supply most of the rest. No factor is Bullish at this horizon; Policy & Rates, Risk Appetite, Positioning, Market Structure and USD Liquidity are Neutral. The view rests on slow-moving structural gaps, not on near-term events. -0.3147 is at or below -0.10, so the stance is Bearish; conviction is 3 because three independent channels point the same way.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, External Balance (0.19), Policy & Rates (0.24) and Guidance (0.12) are the heaviest factors. Two of the three are Bearish, giving a net score of -0.315. External Balance carries the most signal: the euro area's 12-month surplus has fallen to 1.5% of GDP and is heading towards about 1.0%, with gas about three times its pre-war level, while Singapore's second-quarter surplus rose 21% on a year earlier on electronics exports. Guidance adds a two-sided mismatch: the euro curve prices about 75bp of ECB tightening against our expected 50bp, with Lagarde leaving on 7 February 2027, while MAS's warning of upside inflation risks makes a tightening more likely than an easing, which forwards do not price. Our two standalone views agree: the euro ranks 10th of 11 strategically and the Singapore dollar 3rd, one of the widest gaps among euro crosses. Factors specific to this pair modify both: the cross removes the US dollar funding question, and the euro's carry lead, which hurts a euro holder against the US dollar, helps one against the Singapore dollar. The main counterweight is valuation. The Singapore dollar's real effective rate is at the 88th percentile of its recent range against the euro's 67th, which limits how far Singapore's advantage can be pressed. Policy & Rates stays Neutral because the 120bp carry is offset by the band's appreciation. What is priced is a December ECB hike, an unchanged MAS band and both external balances as they stand today. Our edge is the euro area's continuing erosion and the ECB under-delivering against pricing. The path of least resistance is lower through the winter gas season. Key checkpoints are the 17 December ECB decision with projections, the French budget deadline the same day, the 9 December FOMC through its effect on SORA, and MAS's next statement, expected in late January with no verified date. Conviction is 3 because three independent channels point the same way: energy terms of trade, French fiscal politics, and the gap between guidance and pricing. It is not 4 because a US-Iran settlement would hit the energy channel hard, and record euro shorts could front-load a rally.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, EUR/SGD ranks among the top three euro shorts, alongside EUR/NOK and EUR/CAD, because it pairs the second-weakest structural profile (the euro, 10th of 11) with the third-strongest (the Singapore dollar, 3rd of 11). Unlike EUR/NOK it does not depend on oil staying high, since Singapore's surplus rests on electronics. Among Singapore dollar longs it ranks first: USD/SGD forwards already price most of the band's appreciation, and SGD/NOK and AUD/SGD run against commodity carry. Its drawback against EUR/GBP and EUR/NOK is that a short pays carry instead of earning it.

conditions: TTF averages EUR80-100/MWh through the winter.
The ECB hikes to 2.75% on 17 December and at most once more by March 2027.
MAS holds the band in January and April with the slope near 1.25% a year.
The OAT-Bund spread averages 150-170bp into the May 2027 election.
base_case.path: -274 pips (-1.92%) from spot 1.42738. The pair reaches the round number inside the three-touch 1.3991-1.40314 band (the February 2025 low) via a staircase lower of about 45 pips a month, with rallies capped at 1.4366-1.4502.

conditions: A US-Iran settlement reopens Hormuz and takes TTF below EUR70/MWh.
MAS cuts the band slope by April as AI exports slow sharply, or the ECB signals hikes beyond 3.00%.

A French government collapse with the OAT-Bund spread above 190bp. MUFG's fiscal-drift scenario is the reference: MUFG assigns a 45% probability to continued fiscal drift as France approaches its presidential election. In that scenario, MUFG envisages EUR/USD at 1.08-1.14, while the extra yield investors demand to hold French rather than German ten-year government debt widens to around 170 basis points.
TTF above EUR120/MWh in a cold winter, with MAS adding slope in January.

strategic.path_expectation: November to 17 December: the pair trades 1.4160-1.4410. The French votes and the S&P review break the 1.41985 floor, and rallies are capped at the ten-touch band. 17 December to mid-January: the ECB decision and the French constitutional deadline fall on the same day. That is the inflection: a hike framed as the last, plus a missed deadline, takes the pair to 1.4100, while a hawkish projection round produces a 100-150 pip squeeze back towards 1.4250. Late January to April: the MAS statement, euro-area fourth-quarter GDP (around 29 January), the euro-area HICP peak and the ECB leadership change should extend a grind of about 45 pips a month to 1.4000 by late April, with pullbacks capped at 1.4366-1.4502. Realised volatility should run at 3-4%. The pattern is a staircase lower, not a collapse, unless the French downside scenario materialises.

increase_conditions: Increase to 4 if the 17 December ECB projections show 2027 core HICP at or below 2.5% and the ECB signals a pause after one hike, with a weekly close below 1.4100, or MAS adds slope in January.
Increase to 5 if the euro-area current account shows a monthly deficit for two consecutive months while Singapore's third-quarter current account exceeds S$40bn.
decrease_conditions: Decrease to 2 if there is a weekly close above 1.4502 (the top of the ten-touch band), or TTF stays below EUR70/MWh for two weeks.
Decrease to 1 if there is a weekly close above the 200-week average (1.4625 now, about 1.4683 by late April), or MAS cuts the band slope.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: No bank forecast published specifically for EUR/SGD was found. Crossing MUFG Research's November 2026 forecasts (EUR/USD 1.12 at end-Q4 2026 and 1.14 at end-Q1 2027; USD/SGD 1.2750 and 1.2700) implies EUR/SGD of about 1.428 at end-2026 and about 1.448 at end-March 2027. Crossing ING's October forecasts (EUR/USD 1.13 for Q4; USD/SGD 1.28 at one to three months and 1.27 at six months) and the Reuters poll median of 1.15 for EUR/USD at three to six months gives a similar flat-to-higher path of roughly 1.44-1.46. All of these are derived crosses, not published EUR/SGD forecasts.
consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: MUFG Research, Monthly Foreign Exchange Outlook, November 2026 (cross derived from its EUR/USD and USD/SGD forecasts); ING Think, FX Talking, October 2026, and the Reuters FX poll of 30 September-2 October as reported by NAGA (cross derived from their EUR/USD and USD/SGD figures).
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bearish EUR/SGD over four weeks (score -0.215, conviction 2): euro-area stagflation, French fiscal events and the energy terms-of-trade gap outweigh a crowded short. Target 1.4160 by 27 November.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish EUR/SGD over the strategic horizon (score -0.315, conviction 3): diverging external balances, ECB pricing ahead of its guidance, and the fiscal gap. Target 1.4000 by 30 April 2027.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Below consensus: the derived bank paths are flat to higher, and we expect the pair to fall.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: We disagree on direction, not just size. The derived bank paths sit roughly at spot for end-2026 and about 1.4% above it by end-March 2027, while we expect a decline. At six months our 1.4000 target is about 450 pips (3.1%) below the derived MUFG cross.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The bank paths come from US dollar forecasts that assume a euro recovery driven by ECB hikes and a Singapore dollar that only edges higher against the US dollar. We weigh three bilateral factors more heavily. The external balances are moving in opposite directions under a gas shock that the early-October forecasts largely predate, since gas rose about 39% between 30 September and 28 October. We think ECB pricing is about 25bp too high, so rate support for the euro fades. And French fiscal and political risk has moved from a spread problem towards a euro problem since mid-October. We also count MAS's hawkish bias under an unchanged band, which a fixed-band assumption ignores. Other published views: the MUFG path rests on a euro recovery (forecast 1.12 for the final quarter of this year, then a gradual recovery to 1.18 by September 2027) that depends on French risks easing and on ECB quarter-point increases in December 2026 and March 2027 taking the deposit rate to 3.00%; on the Singapore side MUFG projects USD/SGD at 1.26 by the third quarter of 2027, and BofA sees inflation bringing renewed policy tightening in January, a Singapore-side risk to our view that runs the other way. The one published pair-specific call we found points the same way as ours with similar levels (base case 1.4172 by December 17, 2026; bull case 1.4460; bear case 1.4061; invalidation above 1.4395), close to our tactical 1.4160 target and 1.4415 stop. Where we doubt our own call: our disagreement with ourselves is about timing, not direction. Spot is at the 1st percentile of its 52-week closing range, sits inside its only nearby support band, and is shorted through both legs. The probability-weighted case for lower levels stands, but a short entered at spot is poorly rewarded, and the first half of November is when the call is most likely to look wrong.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the euro area's external balance keeps eroding and the ECB under-delivers on 17 December, the cross should decline as bank forecasts are cut, and a short position would beat the forward by more than its carry cost of about 14 pips a month.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If a US-Iran settlement pulls gas prices down sharply or the French budget passes cleanly, the record euro short would cover quickly and the pair would rise towards the bank paths. A short would then lose on spot and also pay about 120bp a year in carry.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Bearish, but different factors drive them. Tactically the score comes from the growth-inflation gap and a group of dated French events, and the crowded short (positioning is the only Bullish factor) keeps conviction at 2. Strategically the heavier weights on External Balance and Guidance take over, positioning turns Neutral, and the score deepens to -0.315 at conviction 3.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 17 December 2026 ECB decision with staff projections. A hike with a signal of more to come would weaken the strategic Guidance case; a hike presented as the last would strengthen it. MAS's next statement, expected in late January with no verified date on file, is the Singapore-side checkpoint.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Expect short-covering rallies in the first half of November, driven by the crowded euro short, without treating them as a change in direction. The strategic view is the higher-conviction one, and it is driven by the external balance and the 17 December projections rather than by four-week data. In practice, rallies into 1.4330-1.4450 are where the tactical and strategic shorts are built. A daily close above 1.4415 stops the tactical leg; only a weekly close above 1.4510 stops the strategic leg.

catalysts.event: US midterm elections; French National Assembly vote on the revenue half of the 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: The US has said strikes on Iran would not come before the midterms, so the result opens a window for escalation that would raise oil and gas prices. Both oil importers would suffer, but the euro more, through TTF gas and French spreads. The same day's French vote is the first test of whether the government has a majority, and it affects only the euro.

Consensus is 3.9% after 3.8% in September. A firm core print would lock in the December ECB hike, which helps the euro's carry, but an energy-driven headline deepens the real-income squeeze. Because the S$NEER band absorbs Singapore data surprises, this release moves EUR/SGD more than any Singapore print in the window.

catalysts.event: French National Assembly vote on the whole 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: Prediction markets gave a budget by year-end only a 44.5% chance on 31 October. Forcing it through without a vote would trigger an immediate censure motion. A failed vote would push the French-German spread back towards its October 15-year high and add to the euro's fiscal discount, with no Singapore-side equivalent. A daily close below 1.41985 around this vote is our signal for the tactical base case.

catalysts.event: Singapore October non-oil domestic exports (typical release slot; date not confirmed on an official calendar)
catalysts.rationale: September exports rose 68.4% y/y on a 107.6% jump in electronics. A print above +40% would confirm the widening surplus behind the strategic External Balance factor. A sharp slowdown below +20% would be the first sign that the AI export cycle is turning, which would weaken the Singapore dollar's structural support.

catalysts.event: Singapore October CPI and MAS core inflation (typical release slot; date not confirmed on an official calendar)
catalysts.rationale: Core inflation eased to 2.0% in September. A rise to 2.3% would revive expectations of a tightening at MAS's next statement and lower EUR/SGD. A print of 1.8% or below would push the S$NEER towards the middle of its band and lift the pair, triggering the positioning unwind risk.

catalysts.event: ECB account of the October monetary policy meeting
catalysts.rationale: The account will show how many members favoured a hike and whether the terminal rate was discussed. A hawkish tone could add a few basis points to December pricing, too little to move the euro's carry lead over the Singapore dollar much. A sign that December is seen as the last hike would matter more.

catalysts.event: S&P Global review of France (A+ stable)
catalysts.rationale: Moody's affirmed France at Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October, on the condition that a deficit-reducing budget is adopted. S&P could move to a negative outlook if the budget stalls. That would widen French spreads and the euro's fiscal discount against a AAA-rated Singapore.

Unemployment rose to 6.5% in September from 6.3% a year earlier. A rise to 6.6% would confirm a weakening labour market ahead of the ECB's December projections and support the case that the ECB stops early. Singapore's unemployment rate of 2.0% shows how wide the gap between the two labour markets is.

A Fed hike to 4.00-4.25% has a probability of about 77%. For this cross the main effect runs through SORA, which follows US rates in part, so a hike narrows the euro's carry lead slightly. Both legs face similar dollar-funding effects, which largely cancel.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with staff projections
catalysts.rationale: This is the only scheduled policy decision for either currency before March. Our euro view expects a 25bp hike to 2.75%, which would lift the euro's lead over SORA to about 145bp. The 2027 inflation projections will decide whether markets keep pricing about 75bp of total tightening, and a hike presented as the last would hurt the euro. No verified MAS schedule is on file: its next statement is expected in late January but has no confirmed date, so it is not listed here as a dated catalyst.

catalysts.event: French constitutional deadline for Parliament to pass the 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: Missing the deadline would mean enactment by ordinance or a stopgap special law, either of which would undermine the 5.0% deficit target. Falling on the same day as the ECB decision, it could compound a dovish surprise and widen the euro's fiscal discount against Singapore's AAA surplus.

assumptions: Daily closing prices cover 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 1.42738 at the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November is a Sunday, so the gap is two calendar days with no trading session missed. All levels, pips and percentages are measured from that close.
No weekend bars were in the series. Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes.

Moving averages, the 200-week average and its slope, and the support and resistance bands are computed over the full stored history: 4,919 weekday sessions from 24 December 2007 to 30 October 2026, which also give 1,010 weekly and 502 monthly bars.
Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 64 pips.

The 52-week percentile quoted in the text is on closing prices (1st percentile); on intraday highs and lows it is the 3rd. The structured range fields use the closing range (1.42666-1.51694); the intraday range is 1.42400-1.52175.

Only six resistance bands and two support bands met the two-touch threshold. Support was supplemented with round numbers (1.4200, 1.4100, 1.4000), which carry no measured touch count, and with the 2022 cycle low near 1.3720 from third-party commentary. Bands are ranked by touch count, not proximity.
Band distances are given to both the near edge and the midpoint. The midpoint figures match the computed distances.

Singapore has no policy rate because MAS targets the S$NEER band, and the price dataset has no Singapore policy-rate or 10-year series. Three-month compounded SORA (1.297% on 30 October) is used as the Singapore short rate (the quote_policy_rate field).
The 120bp carry is a gap between short rates, not a funding gap implied by quoted forwards. The forward outrights in this report are indicative values derived from that gap, not market quotes.

The German 10-year figure of 3.47% in the rate dataset is a September monthly average and is not quoted as a live level. The 10-year comparison uses the 30 October daily closes of 3.32% (Bund) and 2.24% (Singapore government bond).

No implied volatility exists for EUR/SGD on any exchange or free source, so implied-volatility percentiles, the variance risk premium and the implied carry-to-vol ratio are left blank rather than estimated. Carry over realised volatility (about 0.43) is shown only as a labelled substitute.
CFTC percentile ranks for euro positioning are not given in the report and are left null; Singapore dollar has no reportable futures positioning.
No forward funding differential or EUR/SGD cross-currency basis is published.
One decision for the two currencies falls before 1 March 2027: the ECB on 17 December 2026, with projections. MAS's next statement is expected in late January without a verified date.
Singapore's November export and CPI release dates are typical slots, not confirmed dates.

No bank forecast specific to EUR/SGD was found. Consensus is derived by crossing published EUR/USD and USD/SGD forecasts from MUFG, ING and the Reuters poll. Model-generated forecast sites were excluded. One independent pair-specific commentary is referenced alongside.
Bilateral goods trade is IMF data for 2024 in US dollars. Euro-area and Singapore records differ because of re-export accounting, but both show a euro-area surplus of about $10-11bn.
Singapore dollar positioning uses the OCBC S$NEER estimate and MAS reserve changes as proxies. The band slope of about 1.25% a year is a UOB estimate from July.
Weights were adjusted on three factors: External Balance +0.03, Fiscal +0.02 and USD Liquidity -0.05 on both horizons. Both horizons sum to 1.00.

Factor stances rest on rates, macro data, policy communication, positioning, trade balances, geopolitics, valuation and cross-asset evidence. The pair's own price history enters only Factor 9 and the trade plan: entries, targets, stops, sizing and scenario levels.

Event and meeting probabilities come from our euro and Singapore assessments. Where they differ, as on the odds of a post-midterm US strike on Iran (35% and 20%), both figures are reported. Scenario probabilities are our own.
Metadata dossier dates are set to the valuation date as the report does not state separate dossier dates.
